# Shield Connector Structure and Assembly

## Overview

The shield connector (1) incorporates a multi-layered protective and grounding structure designed to secure electrical wires (W) while providing electromagnetic shielding and environmental sealing. This structure is composed of several key components working in concert: a housing (8), a protective tube (11), a braided wire shield (12), a rubber boot (13), and a shield shell (17). Each component serves a distinct function while maintaining physical and electrical continuity with the others.

## Wire Routing and Initial Shielding

The wires (W) originate from within the housing (8) and extend outward through a tube (11), which serves as a channel or conduit to guide and protect the wires as they exit the housing body. Surrounding these wires, and running along the length of the tube (11), is a braided wire (12). This braided wire functions as an electromagnetic shield, wrapping around the wire bundle to reduce electromagnetic interference and provide grounding continuity.

## Attachment of the Braided Wire

The end portion of the braided wire (12) closest to the housing body is mounted directly onto the tube (11). This mounting arrangement ensures that the braided shield is securely and stably attached at its housing-side terminus, preventing displacement or loosening during operation or handling. This secure attachment point on the tube (11) establishes a fixed reference for the braided wire's position relative to the housing body.

## Rubber Boot Placement

Layered over the braided wire (12) is a rubber boot (13). This boot is positioned to cover both the tube (11) itself and the sections of the wires (W) that extend out from the tube. By enveloping the tube and wire portions from the outside of the braided wire, the rubber boot (13) provides an additional layer of environmental protection—guarding against moisture, dust, and mechanical stress—while also helping to maintain the position and integrity of the braided wire shield beneath it.

## Shield Shell Coverage

A shield shell (17) is positioned to cover the housing body (9) as well as a portion of the rubber boot (13). This shield shell serves as an outer protective and shielding structure, extending coverage from the housing body outward to overlap with part of the boot assembly. The rubber boot (13) is fixed to this shield shell (17), creating a secure mechanical connection between the two components and ensuring that the boot remains properly seated and stationary relative to the shield shell during use.

## Integration of the Braided Wire with the Shield Shell

A critical feature of this design is the manner in which the braided wire (12) integrates with the shield shell (17). The end part of the braided wire (12) on the housing body side is routed through an opening formed in the rubber boot (13). Upon passing through this opening, the braided wire's end becomes sandwiched—held firmly in place—between the rubber boot (13) and the shield shell (17). 

This sandwiching arrangement accomplishes two functions simultaneously: it mechanically secures the braided wire's end in a fixed position by capturing it between two adjacent components, and it establishes reliable electrical contact between the braided wire (12) and the shield shell (17), ensuring continuous shielding and effective grounding pathways throughout the connector assembly. This design allows for a compact, integrated structure where sealing, shielding, and mechanical retention are achieved through the coordinated interaction of the rubber boot and shield shell components.

# Electromagnetic Shielding Connector for Wire Harness Applications

## Background and Technical Field

In modern electrical and electronic systems, wires and cables that exit a housing often require protection from electromagnetic interference (EMI) to maintain signal integrity and comply with electromagnetic compatibility (EMC) standards. This is particularly critical in automotive, aerospace, industrial control, and telecommunications applications, where sensitive signal-carrying conductors must be shielded from external electromagnetic noise while also preventing the wires themselves from emitting interference that could disrupt nearby electronic components.

A common challenge in connector design involves maintaining continuous, reliable shielding at the point where wires transition from an enclosed housing, through a protective tube, and out into the external environment. Traditional shielding solutions often suffer from gaps in shielding coverage, unreliable electrical grounding connections, or mechanical designs that are difficult to assemble consistently, all of which can compromise the overall effectiveness of the EMI shielding system.

## Overview of the Shield Connector Assembly

The shield connector described herein provides a robust and effective solution for maintaining electromagnetic shielding integrity for wires that pass through a housing and exit via a tubular extension. The assembly comprises several key components working together to form a continuous shielding pathway:

**1. Braided Wire Shielding**

A braided wire—typically constructed from fine metallic strands woven into a flexible mesh—surrounds the individual wires as they pass through the tube portion of the housing. This braided shielding material is well-suited for EMI suppression due to its excellent conductivity, flexibility, and ability to conform around the wire bundle while providing 360-degree coverage against electromagnetic radiation.

**2. Rubber Boot**

A rubber boot is positioned to cover both the tube portion of the housing and the corresponding section of the braided wire shielding. This boot serves multiple functions: it provides environmental sealing against moisture, dust, and other contaminants; it offers mechanical protection and strain relief for the wires and braided shield; and, critically, it plays an integral role in maintaining the electrical continuity of the shielding system, as will be described in detail below.

**3. Shield Shell**

Enclosing the primary housing body and the rubber boot is a shield shell, typically constructed from a conductive metal or metallized material. This outer shell serves as the primary structural and electromagnetic barrier, providing a low-impedance path to ground and completing the overall shielding enclosure around the connector assembly.

## Key Innovation: Sandwiched Braided Wire Connection

The core innovation of this shield connector design lies in the specific method by which electrical continuity is established and maintained between the braided wire shield and the outer shield shell. Rather than relying on a separate clamping mechanism, solder joint, or additional fastening hardware—approaches that can introduce assembly complexity, increase manufacturing costs, or create potential points of failure—this design achieves a secure electrical connection through a simple yet highly effective sandwiching technique.

Specifically, the housing-side end of the braided wire (i.e., the end nearest to the main housing body, as opposed to the end that extends further along the tube toward the wire exit point) is positioned so that it becomes trapped, or "sandwiched," between the outer surface of the rubber boot and the inner surface of the shield shell during final assembly.

This sandwiching arrangement offers several distinct advantages:

- **Secure Electrical Contact**: By compressing the braided wire end between the rubber boot and the shield shell, consistent and firm physical contact is maintained between the conductive braided material and the conductive shield shell, ensuring reliable electrical continuity.

- **Simplified Assembly**: This design eliminates the need for additional connection hardware, separate grounding clips, or complex soldering operations, as the sandwiching action naturally occurs as part of the standard assembly process when the shield shell is installed over the boot and housing.

- **Consistent Manufacturing**: Because the connection relies on the geometric relationship between the components rather than a separate assembly step prone to human error or variability, the design promotes consistent, repeatable shielding performance across production runs.

- **Mechanical Stability**: The rubber boot's inherent flexibility and compressive properties help maintain consistent pressure on the braided wire against the shield shell, even under varying environmental conditions such as temperature fluctuations or mechanical vibration.

## Resulting Benefits

By integrating these components into a unified assembly—the braided wire providing localized shielding around the wire bundle, the rubber boot providing sealing and mechanical support while facilitating the critical grounding connection, and the shield shell providing overall structural and electromagnetic enclosure—this connector design achieves continuous, uninterrupted shielding coverage from the point where wires exit the housing through the tube to their final termination point.

This continuous shielding pathway is essential for preventing electromagnetic leakage at transition points, which are often the weakest links in conventional shielding designs. The sandwiched connection between the braided wire and shield shell ensures that the shielding effectiveness of the entire assembly is not compromised by poor grounding or intermittent electrical contact, thereby providing a reliable, durable, and manufacturable solution for EMI shielding in wire harness and connector applications.

# The Word "The"

"The" is often called the most common word in the English language—and for good reason. It appears more frequently in written and spoken English than any other word, showing up roughly once in every 20 words we use.

## A Small Word with Big Grammatical Power

"The" is what linguists call a **definite article**. Its job is to point to something specific—a particular noun that both the speaker and listener already have in mind. Compare these two sentences:

- "I saw a dog in the park." (an unspecified dog, somewhere unspecified)
- "I saw the dog in the park." (a specific dog we both know about, in a specific park)

That tiny shift from "a" to "the" changes the entire meaning of the sentence, signaling shared knowledge or a previously mentioned subject.

## Origins

The word traces its roots back to Old English, descending from the word "þe" or "se," related to demonstrative pronouns like "that" and "this." Over centuries, it evolved into the simple, three-letter word we use today.

## Why It's Tricky for Language Learners

Many languages—like Russian, Japanese, and Mandarin—don't have articles at all. This makes "the" (along with "a" and "an") one of the most challenging aspects of English for non-native speakers to master. There's no simple rule that covers every case; much of correct article usage comes down to convention and practice rather than logic.

## A Word That Disappears in Plain Sight

Despite its outsized presence in our language, "the" is rarely noticed. It carries no vivid imagery, no emotional weight, no distinct sound that draws attention to itself. Yet remove it from a sentence, and the sentence often falls apart or loses clarity. It's the scaffolding of English—invisible, indispensable, and everywhere.

In many ways, "the" represents how the most essential parts of language are often the ones we take most for granted.

# ABSTRACT

A shield connector assembly is disclosed for providing electromagnetic shielding to a plurality of wires extending from a housing. The assembly includes a housing having a wire extension portion through which a plurality of wires pass, the wires extending outwardly from the housing along a tubular passage. A braided wire member is disposed about the wires so as to circumferentially surround and shield the wires as they exit the tube, the braided wire member being formed of a plurality of interwoven electrically conductive strands providing electromagnetic interference shielding along the length of the exposed wires. A shield shell is mounted to the housing and is configured to electrically and mechanically engage a first end portion of the braided wire member, thereby establishing electrical continuity between the braided wire member and the shield shell. A rubber boot is fitted over at least a second end portion of the braided wire member and a portion of the tube, the rubber boot being configured to compress the braided wire member against an outer surface of the tube so as to retain the braided wire member in position and to provide a watertight and dust-resistant seal between the wires, the tube, and the braided wire member. The rubber boot further extends over the wires exiting the tube to protect the wires from external environmental exposure while maintaining flexibility to accommodate wire movement. The shield shell, braided wire member, and rubber boot cooperate to form a continuous shielding and sealing structure that inhibits electromagnetic interference from being emitted from or received by the wires, while simultaneously preventing ingress of moisture, dust, and other contaminants into the housing and along the wire extension path. The assembly provides a compact, reliable, and easily assembled shielding structure suitable for use in automotive wiring harnesses and other applications requiring both electromagnetic shielding and environmental sealing of exposed conductor bundles.

# UNITED STATES PATENT APPLICATION

## ELECTRICAL SHIELD CONNECTOR ASSEMBLY

---

### FIELD OF THE INVENTION

The present invention relates generally to electrical connector assemblies, and more particularly to a shielded electrical connector component providing electromagnetic interference (EMI) suppression through an integrated housing, tube, braided wire, rubber boot, and shield shell configuration for use in high-frequency signal transmission applications.

---

### BACKGROUND OF THE INVENTION

Electrical connectors used in signal transmission environments are frequently susceptible to electromagnetic interference, which may degrade signal integrity, introduce noise, or cause cross-talk between adjacent conductive paths. Conventional shielding solutions often suffer from inadequate grounding continuity, insufficient strain relief at cable-connector junctions, and mechanical vulnerability to moisture ingress and vibration-induced fatigue. There exists a need for an improved shielded connector assembly that provides robust EMI attenuation while maintaining mechanical durability, environmental sealing, and ease of manufacture.

---

### SUMMARY OF THE INVENTION

In accordance with the present invention, there is provided an electrical shield connector assembly comprising a housing defining an internal cavity for receiving one or more electrical contacts; a tube disposed at least partially within the housing and configured to receive and guide a cable therethrough; a braided wire surrounding at least a portion of the tube and electrically coupled to a shield shell to establish a continuous grounding path; a rubber boot disposed about a rearward portion of the assembly to provide strain relief and environmental sealing; and a shield shell substantially enclosing the housing and electrically connected to the braided wire, thereby forming a Faraday-cage-like structure that attenuates electromagnetic interference while maintaining mechanical integrity of the cable-connector interface.

---

### DETAILED DESCRIPTION OF THE PREFERRED EMBODIMENT

Referring now to the drawings, wherein like reference numerals refer to like elements throughout the several views, there is shown in **FIG. 1** an electrical shield connector assembly, generally designated **10**, constructed in accordance with the principles of the present invention.

**The Housing**

The assembly **10** includes a housing **20** fabricated from a dielectric, electrically insulative material, such as a thermoplastic polymer, and defining a front mating face **22** and a rear cable-receiving face **24**. The housing **20** further defines an internal cavity **26** extending longitudinally therethrough, said cavity **26** being configured to receive and retain one or more electrical contacts **28** in a predetermined spatial arrangement. The housing **20** comprises an outer peripheral surface **30** having a plurality of retention features **32**, such as detents, ribs, or snap-fit tabs, configured to engage corresponding structures on the shield shell **70**, as described in greater detail below. The housing **20** may further define a keying feature **34** to ensure proper orientation during mating engagement with a complementary connector.

**The Tube**

Disposed at least partially within the rear cable-receiving face **24** of the housing **20** is a tube **40**, said tube **40** defining a longitudinal bore **42** dimensioned to receive a cable **12** therethrough. The tube **40** is preferably formed from an electrically conductive material, such as a metal or metal-plated polymer, and comprises a forward end **44** in electrical and mechanical engagement with the housing **20** and/or the shield shell **70**, and a rearward end **46** extending outwardly from the housing **20**. The tube **40** functions to provide mechanical support to the cable **12** at the point of entry into the housing **20**, thereby reducing bending stress and preventing kinking of the cable **12** during use. In certain embodiments, the tube **40** further comprises a crimping region **48** proximate the rearward end **46**, configured to receive a portion of the braided wire **50**, as discussed below.

**The Braided Wire**

A braided wire **50**, comprising a plurality of interwoven electrically conductive strands, such as tinned copper or copper alloy filaments, is disposed circumferentially about at least a portion of the tube **40**. The braided wire **50** extends longitudinally from a first end **52**, disposed proximate the crimping region **48** of the tube **40**, to a second end **54**, disposed in electrical contact with the shield shell **70**. The braided wire **50** is affixed to the tube **40** by a crimping ferrule **56**, soldering, or other suitable mechanical and electrical joining method, such that a low-impedance electrical path is established between the cable's shielding layer (not shown), the tube **40**, and the shield shell **70**. This continuous conductive path facilitates the dissipation of electromagnetic energy and provides a grounding continuity essential to effective EMI suppression.

**The Rubber Boot**

A rubber boot **60**, formed from an elastomeric material such as silicone rubber, neoprene, or thermoplastic elastomer, is disposed about the rearward end **46** of the tube **40** and at least a portion of the braided wire **50**. The rubber boot **60** defines an internal bore **62** configured to circumferentially engage the cable **12** and the tube **40**, thereby providing strain relief against bending, torsional, and axial forces exerted upon the cable **12** during installation and service. The rubber boot **60** further comprises a sealing lip **64** disposed at an interface with the shield shell **70**, said sealing lip **64** configured to prevent ingress of moisture, dust, and other environmental contaminants into the internal cavity **26** of the housing **20**. In a preferred embodiment, the rubber boot **60** is overmolded directly onto the tube **40** and the braided wire **50**, thereby forming a unitary, environmentally sealed structure.

**The Shield Shell**

A shield shell **70**, fabricated from an electrically conductive material such as stamped and formed sheet metal, die-cast metal alloy, or metallized plastic, at least partially encloses the housing **20**, the tube **40**, and a portion of the braided wire **50** and rubber boot **60**. The shield shell **70** comprises a forward portion **72** configured to engage the outer peripheral surface **30** of the housing **20**, and a rearward portion **74** configured to receive and retain the rubber boot **60** and to establish electrical contact with the second end **54** of the braided wire **50**. The shield shell **70** further defines one or more latching members **76** configured to releasably engage a complementary mating shield shell of an opposing connector, thereby establishing continuous shield-to-shield electrical continuity across the mated connector interface. In this manner, the shield shell **70**, in cooperation with the braided wire **50** and the tube **40**, forms a substantially continuous electromagnetic shield extending from the cable **12** through the connector assembly **10** and across the mating interface, thereby minimizing electromagnetic emission and susceptibility to external interference.

**Assembly Relationships**

It will be appreciated that the housing **20**, tube **40**, braided wire **50**, rubber boot **60**, and shield shell **70** cooperate to form an integrated assembly in which:

1. the housing **20** provides dielectric isolation and mechanical retention for the electrical contacts **28**;
2. the tube **40** provides mechanical guidance and support for the cable **12** while establishing a first segment of the electromagnetic shielding path;
3. the braided wire **50** provides a flexible, low-impedance electrical connection bridging the tube **40** and the shield shell **70**;
4. the rubber boot **60** provides strain relief and environmental sealing about the tube **40** and braided wire **50**; and
5. the shield shell **70** provides an outer conductive enclosure electrically continuous with the braided wire **50** and configured for shield continuity across the mating interface.

This cooperative arrangement provides a robust, manufacturable, and effective electrical shield connector assembly suitable for use in demanding electromagnetic environments.

---

### CLAIMS

**1.** An electrical shield connector assembly, comprising:

a tube disposed at least partially within the housing, the tube defining a longitudinal bore configured to receive a cable therethrough;
a braided wire disposed circumferentially about at least a portion of the tube, the braided wire having a first end electrically connected to the tube and a second end electrically connected to a shield shell;
a rubber boot disposed about a rearward portion of the tube and at least a portion of the braided wire, the rubber boot configured to provide strain relief and environmental sealing; and

**3.** The electrical shield connector assembly of claim 1, wherein the braided wire is affixed to the tube by a crimping ferrule.

**4.** The electrical shield connector assembly of claim 1, wherein the rubber boot is overmolded onto the tube and the braided wire to form a unitary sealed structure.

**5.** The electrical shield connector assembly of claim 1, wherein the shield shell comprises a forward portion engaging an outer peripheral surface of the housing and a rearward portion retaining the rubber boot.

**6.** The electrical shield connector assembly of claim 1, wherein the shield shell further comprises at least one latching member configured to releasably engage a complementary shield shell of a mating connector.

**7.** The electrical shield connector assembly of claim 1, wherein the rubber boot further comprises a sealing lip disposed at an interface with the shield shell to prevent ingress of moisture and contaminants.

**8.** The electrical shield connector assembly of claim 1, wherein the housing further comprises a keying feature configured to ensure proper orientation during mating engagement.

**9.** A method of assembling an electrical shield connector, comprising:
inserting a tube into a rear cable-receiving face of a housing;
disposing a braided wire circumferentially about at least a portion of the tube;
electrically and mechanically affixing a first end of the braided wire to the tube;
overmolding a rubber boot about the tube and the braided wire; and
enclosing the housing, tube, and braided wire within a shield shell such that a second end of the braided wire is placed in electrical communication with the shield shell.

**10.** The method of claim 9, further comprising engaging at least one latching member of the shield shell with a complementary shield shell of a mating connector to establish shield-to-shield electrical continuity.

# Wire Shielding Connector Design: Braided Shield Termination

## Overview

This design describes a cable shield termination method where an EMI/RFI braided shield is mechanically captured and electrically grounded through a compression-based sandwich assembly. The core principle relies on controlled compression of the braid between two components: a shield shell (typically metallic, providing 360° grounding) and a rubber boot (providing strain relief, environmental sealing, and mechanical backing).

## Component Breakdown

### 1. Shield Shell
- Typically machined or stamped from conductive metal (brass, aluminum, or beryllium copper for spring applications)
- Features an internal cavity or stepped bore designed to accept the flared/folded-back braid
- May include internal serrations, knurling, or ribbing to increase contact surface area and bite into the braid strands
- Connects to the connector backshell or housing, providing continuous electrical path to the mating shield/ground reference

### 2. Braided Shield (Cable Screen)
- Tinned copper, bare copper, or aluminum braid from the cable's outer shield layer
- Prepared by cutting back the outer jacket to expose braid, then folding/flaring the braid back over the cable jacket (or over an internal ferrule) to create an even, cylindrical presentation surface
- Braid density and fold-back length are critical—insufficient overlap causes intermittent contact; excessive bulk prevents proper seating

### 3. Rubber Boot (Grommet/Sleeve)
- Elastomeric material (typically silicone, EPDM, or neoprene) chosen for temperature range, chemical resistance, and compression set characteristics
- Designed with a slight interference fit diameter relative to the folded braid
- Often tapered or stepped to guide the braid into position during assembly
- Provides secondary function of strain relief and jacket sealing against moisture ingress

## Assembly Sequence

**Step 1 — Cable Preparation**
The outer jacket is stripped to expose a defined length of braid. The braid is combed to remove kinks and ensure uniform strand distribution.

**Step 2 — Braid Flare/Fold-Back**
The braid is flared outward (often over a conical tool or the boot itself) and folded back 180° over the outer jacket, creating a double-layer cylindrical shield surface. This fold-back is essential—it prevents single-strand pull-through and doubles the contact area.

**Step 3 — Boot Insertion**
The rubber boot is slid over the folded-back braid from the rear, or the braid is folded back *over* a pre-positioned boot shoulder. The boot's outer diameter is sized so the braid lies flat against it without excessive stretching (which thins the braid layer and reduces contact pressure).

**Step 4 — Shell Compression**
The shield shell is advanced over the assembly (boot + folded braid) and either:
- Crimped radially (hex or round crimp) using a calibrated crimp tool, or
- Threaded/swaged axially, compressing the braid between the shell's internal wall and the boot's outer surface

This compression sandwiches the braid, creating multiple point contacts between individual braid strands and the shell's internal surface while the rubber boot backs the braid to maintain consistent radial pressure.

## Engineering Considerations

### Electrical Contact
- **Contact resistance** is governed by contact pressure, contact area, and surface finish of the shell bore. Target is typically <10 mΩ for the shield-to-shell interface.
- The rubber boot must have sufficient durometer (often 60-80 Shore A) to transmit crimping force without excessive compression that could cause cold-flow and pressure relaxation over time/temperature cycling.
- Too soft a boot → braid contact pressure relaxes over time (rubber creep), increasing resistance
- Too hard a boot → poor strain relief, cracking under vibration, incomplete braid seating

### Mechanical Retention
- The compressed braid, sandwiched under radial load, acts as a friction-locked collar
- Pull-out force testing (per MIL-DTL-38999 or similar) validates that the boot/shell sandwich alone (before backshell overmold) can withstand specified axial load without shield migration
- Crimp tooling must apply consistent circumferential force—typically via hex crimp dies—to avoid localized high-stress points that could cut braid strands

### Sealing
- Boot compression against the cable jacket (inboard of the braid termination) provides IP-rated sealing (IP67/IP68 in many designs)
- Boot geometry often includes sealing ribs that bite into the jacket OD independent of the braid termination function

### Failure Modes to Design Against
- **Braid strand cutting**: sharp shell edges or excessive crimp force can shear strands, reducing conductor cross-section and increasing resistance
- **Cold flow/relaxation**: rubber boot degradation under thermal cycling reduces contact pressure over service life
- **Braid migration**: inadequate fold-back length allows braid to pull through under cable flex, breaking the ground path
- **Corrosion**: dissimilar metals (e.g., tinned copper braid vs. bare brass shell) in humid environments cause galvanic corrosion, degrading contact over time; plating selection matters

## Typical Materials Summary

| Component | Common Materials |
|---|---|
| Shield Shell | Brass (nickel or tin plated), Aluminum alloy |
| Braid | Tinned Cu, Bare Cu, Al braid |
| Boot | Silicone, EPDM, Neoprene, Fluorosilicone (harsh environments) |

counterfactuals.output:
# TECHNICAL SUMMARY OF SHIELD CONNECTOR INVENTION

## Field of the Invention

The present invention relates to a shield connector (1) for use in connecting shielded electrical wires, particularly for automotive wire harness applications, wherein electromagnetic shielding continuity is maintained through a conductive housing arrangement.

## Summary of Structural Components

**Connector Housing (1)**

The shield connector (1) comprises a housing body configured to accommodate one or more terminal-fitted wires therein. The housing (1) defines a wire insertion cavity extending along a longitudinal axis and is formed of an insulating synthetic resin material, within which the conductive components described below are retained.

**Shield Shell (8)**

A shield shell (8), formed from an electrically conductive material such as sheet metal, is disposed so as to at least partially surround the outer periphery of the connector housing (1). The shield shell (8) is configured to electromagnetically shield the terminal fittings and wire connection portions housed within the connector housing (1), thereby suppressing electromagnetic noise emission and ingress. The shield shell (8) includes a tubular or box-like main body portion having an open end for receiving a mating connector, and is provided with engagement features for securing it to the housing (1).

**Braided Wire Connection Member (11)**

A braided wire (11), constituting the shielding conductor of a shielded electrical wire, is drawn out from an end of the shielded wire and folded back or crimped so as to establish electrical continuity with the shield shell (8). The braided wire (11) is positioned so as to be electrically and mechanically connected to a connecting portion of the shield shell (8), thereby extending the shielding effect from the wire itself into the connector assembly.

**Retaining Member / Clamp Ring (12)**

A retaining member (12), which may be embodied as a clamp ring or crimping ring, is fitted over the folded-back portion of the braided wire (11) so as to press and fix the braided wire (11) against the connecting portion of the shield shell (8). The retaining member (12) is preferably crimped radially inward to establish a firm mechanical grip and reliable electrical contact between the braided wire (11) and the shield shell (8).

**Rear Holder (13)**

A rear holder (13) is mounted to a rear end portion of the connector housing (1) so as to cover and protect the connection region between the braided wire (11), the retaining member (12), and the shield shell (8). The rear holder (13) is configured to be assembled onto the housing (1) from the rear side, in the wire-drawing direction, and includes locking means (e.g., resilient lock arms or lances) for engaging corresponding lock receiving portions formed on the housing (1) and/or the shield shell (8), thereby retaining the rear holder (13) in an assembled state.

**Sealing/Retaining Member (17)**

A further member (17), which may be constituted as a rubber plug, seal member, or a wire cover component, is provided at a position rearward of the rear holder (13) or integrated therewith, so as to seal the wire lead-out opening and/or to bundle and retain the shielded wires exiting the connector, thereby preventing entry of water, dust, or other foreign matter into the interior of the shield connector (1).

## Assembly Relationship

In the assembled state, the connector housing (1) receives the terminal-equipped ends of the shielded wires therein, with the shield shell (8) fitted over the housing (1) so as to enclose the terminal accommodating region. The braided wire (11) of each shielded wire is folded back over an outer connecting barrel or tubular portion of the shield shell (8), and the retaining member (12) is crimped thereover to establish a reliable electrical and mechanical connection. The rear holder (13) is subsequently assembled to the rear end of the housing (1)/shield shell (8) assembly so as to enclose and protect the braided wire connection, being secured via engagement with locking projections or lock arms. The member (17) is disposed at the rearmost region of the assembly to provide sealing and/or wire retention, completing the shield connector (1) assembly such that a continuous shielding path is formed from the braided wire (11) through the shield shell (8), while the housing (1), rear holder (13), and member (17) cooperate to provide mechanical protection, strain relief, and environmental sealing for the wire connection.

## Technical Effect

This configuration provides a shield connector (1) which maintains reliable electromagnetic shielding continuity between the shielded wire and the shield shell (8) via the braided wire (11) and retaining member (12), while the rear holder (13) and sealing member (17) provide mechanical protection and sealing, resulting in a compact, robust, and easily assembled shielded connection structure suitable for high-reliability applications such as automotive wiring harnesses.
